name: Avestan
confidence_why: Every grammar consulted, from Jackson 1892, Bartholomae 1895 and Reichelt 1909 to Hoffmann and Forssman 2004 and Skjærvø 2003, states that the Avestan accent is not recorded in the texts, and their only positive remarks are indirect inferences about an inherited Indo-Iranian free accent and a stress shift before the enclitics -cā and -cit, which add to rather than contradict an undetermined record.

catalog_quote: Skjærvø 2003, Lesson 1: "STRESS. We know nothing certain about stress in Avestan. For practical purposes a stress rule like that of Latin or Classical Sanskrit may be used, i.e., 1) stress the second-last syllable (the “penultimate”) if it is “heavy,” i.e., has a long vowel (or diphthong) or a short vowel followed by two or more consonants, or if the word has only two syllables ...; 2) stress the third-last syllable (ante-penultimate) if the penultimate is “light,” i.e., has a short vowel followed by one consonant only ... 3) stress the fourth-last syllable if the antepenultimate and penultimate are both light, but put a secondary stress on the penultimate ... It is also possible that some words still had the accent on the final syllable, as in Old Indic ..." new_statements.quote: Der Akzent des Avestischen ist nicht überliefert. Aus einigen lautlichen Erscheinungen können jedoch Schlüsse auf die Akzentstelle des Av. oder seiner Vorstufen gezogen werden. [...] A. Wortakzent in einheitlichen Wortformen. 1. Zwischen akzentuiertem ä i und Tenuis k p t wird uriran. r stimmlos. [...] 2. Vor dem Akzent ist xii für *hi eingetreten [...] B. Wortgruppenakzent bei Antritt von Partikeln. Die Partikeln -cā 'und', -cit 'sogar (usw.)' haben durch ihren Antritt einen Stärke-Akzent auf der vorausgehenden Endsilbe bewirkt; vgl. latein. populus-que gegenüber pópulus. (§ 83, pp. 112-113; scanned text, diacritics in the -cā/-cit sentence restored from the surrounding scanned 'cd'/'cit')
new_statements.translation: The accent of Avestan is not transmitted. From some phonological phenomena, however, conclusions can be drawn about the place of the accent in Avestan or its prestages. [...] A. Word accent in unitary word forms. 1. Between accented ā/i and voiceless stop k p t, Proto-Iranian r becomes voiceless. [...] 2. Before the accent xii has replaced *hi [...] B. Word-group accent on attachment of particles. The particles -cā 'and', -cit 'even (etc.)' by their attachment caused a stress accent on the preceding final syllable; cf. Latin populus-que versus pópulus.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record 'Avestan' carries an empty rule and there are no existing statements. This work explains why: the accent is unattested; it can only be inferred as the inherited Indo-Iranian free accent, plus a stress on the syllable before enclitic -cā/-cit. Compatible with a blank rule; adds the reason and the indirect evidence. Note the archive.org copy is the 1996 first edition (IBS 84, title page 'Innsbruck 1996', ISBN 3-85124-652-7), not the listed 2004 second edition (IBS 115); the § 83 accent section and its wording are from that 1996 printing.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The Avestan accent is not recorded in the texts (the script marks nothing); its position can only be inferred indirectly from sound changes (devoicing of r after the accent, xii-/xš-/x'- before the accent), which point to the inherited, Vedic-type (lexically placed, mobile) Indo-Iranian accent. The only positive placement rule is a word-group one: the enclitics -cā 'and' and -cit 'even' pull a stress accent onto the immediately preceding (final) syllable of the host, with consequent vowel shortening in the antepenult (§ 26 b), -āat- spellings (§ 39) and blocked i-epenthesis (§ 20 e).
new_statements.exceptions: Enclitic-induced shift onto the syllable before -cā/-cit (§ 83 B); dialectal (probably Arachosian) x'- before the accent (§ 83 A 4); traces of older accent alternation in the inflection of pərətu-/pəšu- 'ford' (§ 90).
new_statements.identity_note: Hoffmann & Forssman treat Old Avestan (aav.) and Young Avestan (jav.) together; § 83 A 4 marks the x'- before-accent development as dialectal, 'wohl arachotisch'. The archive.org copy is the 1996 first edition (IBS 84), not the 2004 second edition listed in the citation. The Bopp file is the 1854 English translation (Eastwick) of Vol. I, which discusses 'Zend' only in the sound system and morphology, with no accent material.

sources.citation: Reichelt, Hans. 1909. Awestisches Elementarbuch. Heidelberg: Carl Winter. §§166-171 'Der Akzent', pp. 80-82.
sources.quote: §166: 'Die Betonung ist im Awesta nicht überliefert; doch läßt sich auf Grund einiger Erscheinungen vermuten, daß sie ursprünglich im allgemeinen mit der altindischen übereinstimmte, wenngleich das exspiratorische Element allmählich vorherrschend geworden zu sein scheint.' §168: 'Eine Übereinstimmung zwischen ai. und aw. Wortakzent ergibt sich aus dem Gesetz, daß aw. r hinter dem Hochton tonlos wird: j. vəhrkō, ai. vŕ̥kaḥ ...' §171: long vowel in open penult shortened when an enclitic or secondary suffix shifts the Hochton to the final syllable (caθβaras-ca vs caθβārō).

sources.quote: 'Die Betonung ist in beiden altiranischen Dialekten unbezeichnet geblieben. I. Für das Altpersische ist nichts zu ermitteln. II. Für das Awestische haben wir wenigstens einige Anhaltspunkte, die dafür zeugen, dass die Sprache im Wesentlichen auf dem arischen Betonungsstandpunkt verharrte, wenigstens noch zu der Zeit, da gewisse Lautveränderungen stattfanden ... Ein im Aind. nicht nachweisbares, aber vielleicht indogermanisches Betonungsgesetz ist die Verschiebung des Worttons auf die letzte Silbe beim Antritt von Enclitiken.'

tone.quote: Immediately following the Proto-Indo-Ir. accent rk became hrk and rp became hrp: mahrka- “destruction,” cf. Vedic márka-; vəhrka- “wolf,” cf. Vedic vṛ́ka-; kəhrpəm “body” from *kṛ́pam. Instead of the expected *hrt from *rt we find ṧ: maṧiia- “man,” cf. Vedic mártiya-; aməṧa- “immortal,” cf. Vedic amṛ́ta-. [...] In OAv. the gen. sing. ending -ahiiā is always written with x́ before enclitic -cā “and:” -ax́iiā-cā. This pronunciation may reflect the secondary accentuation *ahi̯á-ca.
